lede: A cell is the smallest unit a living thing is built from, and every part inside it has a job. Animal and plant cells share most of those parts; plant cells add three more. A light microscope and a drop of iodine make them visible on a slide.
can: Name each cell structure and say what it does.
Tell a bacterial cell from a plant or animal cell.
Calculate total magnification and order cell, tissue, organ, organ system.

md: Everything alive is built from cells, and most of them are far too small to see. Under a school microscope an onion skin turns into rows of brick-shaped boxes, each with a wall, a nucleus and a jelly-like inside. Plant cells carry three parts that animal cells do not.

prompt: Which structure controls what enters and leaves a cell?
explain: The membrane is the gate. The wall is outside it and only gives support — and it is not there at all in an animal cell.

md:
Work outwards, and say what each one **does**, because the function is what the mark is for.
**Cell membrane** — controls the substances entering and leaving the cell.
**Cytoplasm** — where the cell's chemical reactions happen.
**Nucleus** — contains the chromosomes, so it controls the cell.
**Nuclear membrane** — the membrane around the nucleus.
**Mitochondria** — where the reactions of respiration occur.

title: Why the wall and the membrane are not the same job
md: The **cell membrane** is a thin living layer that **chooses** what crosses it, which is why every cell has one. The **cellulose cell wall** outside it is a stiff scaffold that lets everything through and only holds its shape.

prompt: Which part of a cell is where its chemical reactions happen?
explain: The cytoplasm. The nucleus controls the cell; mitochondria do respiration.

title: The three plant extras, with their jobs
md:
**Cellulose cell wall** — a stiff layer outside the cell membrane that provides **support**. Bacteria and fungi have walls too, but not made of cellulose.
**Large permanent vacuole** — a liquid-filled space holding **cell sap**; it keeps the cell firm and helps it hold its shape.
**Chloroplasts** — contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.

prompt: Which structure holds cell sap and helps a plant cell keep its shape?
answer: vacuole | large permanent vacuole | the vacuole
explain: The large permanent vacuole. 'Stores water' is usually accepted, but 'support' or 'keeps the cell firm' is the safer answer because it is the function CCEA prints.

prompt: Name two structures you can see here that an animal cell would not have, and say why no chloroplasts are visible even though this is a plant.

md: The onion is a storage bulb underground, so its cells make no chlorophyll — **no chloroplasts**, even though every other plant feature is there. That is exactly the trap CCEA set in March 2026: they asked which structure was *not* in the onion-cell diagram.

A **bacterial cell** is the odd one out. It has a cell wall, but not a cellulose one. It has **no nucleus** — its DNA sits loose in the cytoplasm as a single circle — and it carries small extra rings of DNA called **plasmids**. Three facts, and CCEA has asked for all three.

prompt: A diagram shows a bacterial cell. Which structure is present?
explain: Plasmids are the bacterial giveaway. There is no nucleus and no chloroplast, so neither can be named from the diagram.

title: Summer 2025 B1 Foundation Q1, March 2026 B1 Foundation Q1, Summer 2024 B1 Foundation Q1
md: In Summer 2025 many named the three structures but **swapped cell wall and cell membrane**, and several wrote chloroplast where cytoplasm was wanted; the function of the vacuole was the part most often left blank. In March 2026 candidates missed that the **cell wall provides support**, and fewer could say the chloroplast was the structure absent from an onion cell. In Summer 2024 the diagram was bacterial: nucleus was named easily, **plasmid** was not.

prompt: Which structure is missing from an onion cell?
explain: Chloroplasts. An onion bulb grows underground and makes no chlorophyll.

caption: Six part names and one multiplication — that is the whole of the microscope marks.

md:
To make a **temporary slide**: peel a thin piece of tissue, lay it flat on a **slide**, add one drop of **iodine** solution as a stain so the structures are easier to see, then lower a **coverslip** at an angle so no air bubbles are trapped. Start on the lowest-power objective and focus with the **focusing wheel**.
**Total magnification = eyepiece lens × objective lens.** It is a multiplication both ways: if the total is ×100 and the objective is ×10, the eyepiece is 100 ÷ 10 = ×10.

prompt: A ×10 eyepiece is used with a ×40 objective. The total magnification is ×
explain: 10 × 40 = 400. The answer is a magnification, so it has no unit — write ×400, never 400 mm.

text: From one cell to a whole body

caption: Specialised cell, tissue, organ, organ system — in that order.

md: A **specialised** cell is one with adaptations for a particular job. Many of the same kind together make a **tissue**; different tissues working together make an **organ**; organs working together make an **organ system**. The order is the answer to a whole class of one-mark questions, and it is the frame for the rest of B1.

prompt: Put these in order, smallest first.
explain: Cells build tissues, tissues build organs, organs build systems. One step at a time, never skipping the tissue.

md:
Name the parts of an **animal** and a **plant cell** and give each function.
Say what the **cell wall**, **vacuole** and **chloroplasts** do.
Spot a **bacterial cell** by its **plasmids**.
Work out **total magnification**.
Put **cell, tissue, organ, organ system** in order.

Cells almost always open the paper: three lettered structures named, a table of functions, then two structures a plant cell has and an animal cell does not. Microscopy is examined in Booklet B instead, where the magnification working line earns its own mark. Stuck: name what you can, and write the calculation out in full.
